abstract.text: Rapid progress in machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) has brought increasing attention to the potential impacts of AI technologies on society. In this paper we discuss one such potential impact: the problem of accidents in machine learning systems, defined as unintended and harmful behavior that may emerge from poor design of real-world AI systems. We present a list of five practical research problems related to accident risk, categorized according to whether the problem originates from having the wrong objective function (“avoiding side effects” and “avoiding reward hacking”), an objective function that is too expensive to evaluate frequently (“scalable supervision”), or undesirable behavior during the learning process (“safe exploration” and “distributional shift”). We review previous work in these areas as well as suggesting research directions with a focus on relevance to cutting-edge AI systems. Finally, we consider the high-level question of how to think most productively about the safety of forward-looking applications of AI.

thesis.text: AI accident risk should be addressed through five concrete, experimentally tractable machine-learning problems: avoiding negative side effects, avoiding reward hacking, scalable oversight, safe exploration, and robustness to distributional shift.

question.text: How can accident risk in machine learning systems—unintended and harmful behavior from poor design—be framed as concrete, practically attackable technical problems, and what research directions can address the five categories: negative side effects, reward hacking, scalable oversight, safe exploration, and distributional shift? The hypothesis is that AI safety can be productively studied through current ML/RL problems rather than solely speculative superintelligence scenarios.

sections.summary: The paper motivates AI accident risk as unintended harmful behavior from poor design, distinct from privacy/security/fairness, and argues that this risk should be studied through concrete current ML problems rather than only extreme superintelligence scenarios.
sections.title: Introduction and Motivation

sections.summary: The overview categorizes accident risk by where the process goes wrong: wrong objective function (side effects, reward hacking), too-expensive objective evaluation (scalable oversight), and undesirable learning (safe exploration, distributional shift). It illustrates each with a cleaning robot and identifies trends amplifying these risks.
sections.title: Overview: Five Accident Categories and Trends

sections.summary: Side effects arise when an objective focuses on one task while implicitly expressing indifference to the rest of the environment. The paper surveys ways to define, learn, or penalize impact, use multi-agent models, and reason under reward uncertainty.
sections.title: Avoiding Negative Side Effects

sections.summary: Reward hacking occurs when an agent finds a literal but unintended way to maximize a formal reward. The paper identifies sources including partial observability, complex systems, abstract learned rewards, Goodhart's law, feedback loops, and environmental embedding/wireheading.
sections.title: Reward Hacking: Sources and Examples

source_span.start_text: Here we suggest some preliminary, machine-learning based approaches

sections.summary: The paper proposes machine-learning defenses against reward hacking—adversarial rewards, model lookahead, adversarial blinding, careful engineering, reward capping, counterexample resistance, multiple rewards, reward pretraining, variable indifference, and trip wires—then sketches experiments based on delusion boxes.
sections.title: Reward Hacking: Mitigations and Experiments

sections.summary: Scalable oversight asks how to train agents when the true objective is too expensive to evaluate frequently. Semi-supervised RL lets the agent see reward on only a fraction of timesteps or episodes and aims to learn nearly as well as full supervision.
sections.title: Scalable Oversight: Semi-Supervised RL

source_span.start_text: There are other possible approaches to scalable oversight

sections.summary: Beyond semi-supervised RL, scalable oversight can use distant supervision with weak labels, hierarchical reinforcement learning with delegated sub-agents, and experiments scaling from simple control to Atari and real-world tasks.
sections.title: Scalable Oversight: Other Approaches and Experiments

sections.summary: Safe exploration concerns exploratory actions whose consequences are dangerous or irreversible. The paper reviews risk-sensitive criteria, demonstrations/apprenticeship learning, and uncertainty estimation as ways to reduce catastrophic exploration.
sections.title: Safe Exploration: Problem and Risk-Sensitive Approaches

sections.summary: Additional safe-exploration strategies bound exploration to recoverable regions, use simulations, rely on trusted policy oversight, or query humans. The paper proposes a benchmark suite of varied catastrophic toy environments.
sections.title: Safe Exploration: Bounded, Trusted, and Human Oversight

sections.summary: Distributional shift occurs when training and test distributions differ, often causing confident but wrong predictions. Well-specified approaches use covariate-shift importance weighting, marginal likelihood, and expressive model families.
sections.title: Distributional Shift: Problem and Well-Specified Models

sections.summary: Partially specified models avoid full distributional assumptions by making only structural assumptions. Examples include method of moments, instrumental variables, and unsupervised risk estimation.
sections.title: Distributional Shift: Partially Specified Models

sections.summary: Models can be trained on multiple distributions to improve generalization to novel ones, but detecting and responding to out-of-distribution inputs remains critical. Responses include asking humans, calibrating structured outputs, and deploying conservative policies.
sections.title: Distributional Shift: Multiple Distributions and Response

sections.summary: The paper offers two unifying lenses—counterfactual reasoning and machine learning with contracts—then summarizes approaches and proposes calibration/out-of-distribution speech and other experiments.
sections.title: Distributional Shift: Unifying Views, Summary, and Experiments

sections.summary: The paper situates itself among cyber-physical systems verification, futurist AI-safety communities, other calls for safety research, and adjacent social-impact topics like privacy, fairness, security, abuse, transparency, and policy.
sections.title: Related Efforts

sections.summary: The paper concludes that accidents in ML systems are a concrete threat, and that increasingly autonomous systems need a principled unified approach to safety rather than only ad hoc fixes.
sections.title: Conclusion

abstract.text: Rapid progress in machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) has brought increasing attention to the potential impacts of AI technologies on society. In this paper we discuss one such potential impact: the problem of accidents in machine learning systems, defined as unintended and harmful behavior that may emerge from poor design of real-world AI systems. We present a list of five practical research problems related to accident risk, categorized according to whether the problem originates from having the wrong objective function (“avoiding side effects” and “avoiding reward hacking”), an objective function that is too expensive to evaluate frequently (“scalable supervision”), or undesirable behavior during the learning process (“safe exploration” and “distributional shift”). We review previous work in these areas as well as suggesting research directions with a focus on relevance to cutting-edge AI systems. Finally, we consider the high-level question of how to think most productively about the safety of forward-looking applications of AI.

targets.cited_work: speculative superintelligence-only framings of AI safety

evidence.quote: However, in our opinion one need not invoke these extreme scenarios to productively discuss accidents, and in fact doing so can lead to unnecessarily speculative discussions that lack precision, as noted by some critics [38, 85].

evidence.quote: While many current-day safety problems can and have been handled with ad hoc fixes or case-by-case rules, we believe that the increasing trend towards end-to-end, fully autonomous systems points towards the need for a unified approach to prevent these systems from causing unintended harm.

thesis.text: AI accident risk should be addressed through five concrete, experimentally tractable machine-learning problems: avoiding negative side effects, avoiding reward hacking, scalable oversight, safe exploration, and robustness to distributional shift.

question.text: How can accident risk in machine learning systems—unintended and harmful behavior from poor design—be framed as concrete, practically attackable technical problems, and what research directions can address the five categories: negative side effects, reward hacking, scalable oversight, safe exploration, and distributional shift? The hypothesis is that AI safety can be productively studied through current ML/RL problems rather than solely speculative superintelligence scenarios.

sections.summary: The paper motivates AI accident risk as unintended harmful behavior from poor design, distinct from privacy/security/fairness, and argues that this risk should be studied through concrete current ML problems rather than only extreme superintelligence scenarios.
sections.title: Introduction and Motivation

sections.summary: The overview categorizes accident risk by where the process goes wrong: wrong objective function (side effects, reward hacking), too-expensive objective evaluation (scalable oversight), and undesirable learning (safe exploration, distributional shift). It illustrates each with a cleaning robot and identifies trends amplifying these risks.
sections.title: Overview: Five Accident Categories and Trends

sections.summary: Side effects arise when an objective focuses on one task while implicitly expressing indifference to the rest of the environment. The paper surveys ways to define, learn, or penalize impact, use multi-agent models, and reason under reward uncertainty.
sections.title: Avoiding Negative Side Effects

sections.summary: Reward hacking occurs when an agent finds a literal but unintended way to maximize a formal reward. The paper identifies sources including partial observability, complex systems, abstract learned rewards, Goodhart's law, feedback loops, and environmental embedding/wireheading.
sections.title: Reward Hacking: Sources and Examples

source_span.start_text: Here we suggest some preliminary, machine-learning based approaches

sections.summary: The paper proposes machine-learning defenses against reward hacking—adversarial rewards, model lookahead, adversarial blinding, careful engineering, reward capping, counterexample resistance, multiple rewards, reward pretraining, variable indifference, and trip wires—then sketches experiments based on delusion boxes.
sections.title: Reward Hacking: Mitigations and Experiments

sections.summary: Scalable oversight asks how to train agents when the true objective is too expensive to evaluate frequently. Semi-supervised RL lets the agent see reward on only a fraction of timesteps or episodes and aims to learn nearly as well as full supervision.
sections.title: Scalable Oversight: Semi-Supervised RL

source_span.start_text: There are other possible approaches to scalable oversight

sections.summary: Beyond semi-supervised RL, scalable oversight can use distant supervision with weak labels, hierarchical reinforcement learning with delegated sub-agents, and experiments scaling from simple control to Atari and real-world tasks.
sections.title: Scalable Oversight: Other Approaches and Experiments

sections.summary: Safe exploration concerns exploratory actions whose consequences are dangerous or irreversible. The paper reviews risk-sensitive criteria, demonstrations/apprenticeship learning, and uncertainty estimation as ways to reduce catastrophic exploration.
sections.title: Safe Exploration: Problem and Risk-Sensitive Approaches

sections.summary: Additional safe-exploration strategies bound exploration to recoverable regions, use simulations, rely on trusted policy oversight, or query humans. The paper proposes a benchmark suite of varied catastrophic toy environments.
sections.title: Safe Exploration: Bounded, Trusted, and Human Oversight

sections.summary: Distributional shift occurs when training and test distributions differ, often causing confident but wrong predictions. Well-specified approaches use covariate-shift importance weighting, marginal likelihood, and expressive model families.
sections.title: Distributional Shift: Problem and Well-Specified Models

sections.summary: Partially specified models avoid full distributional assumptions by making only structural assumptions. Examples include method of moments, instrumental variables, and unsupervised risk estimation.
sections.title: Distributional Shift: Partially Specified Models

sections.summary: Models can be trained on multiple distributions to improve generalization to novel ones, but detecting and responding to out-of-distribution inputs remains critical. Responses include asking humans, calibrating structured outputs, and deploying conservative policies.
sections.title: Distributional Shift: Multiple Distributions and Response

sections.summary: The paper offers two unifying lenses—counterfactual reasoning and machine learning with contracts—then summarizes approaches and proposes calibration/out-of-distribution speech and other experiments.
sections.title: Distributional Shift: Unifying Views, Summary, and Experiments

sections.summary: The paper situates itself among cyber-physical systems verification, futurist AI-safety communities, other calls for safety research, and adjacent social-impact topics like privacy, fairness, security, abuse, transparency, and policy.
sections.title: Related Efforts

sections.summary: The paper concludes that accidents in ML systems are a concrete threat, and that increasingly autonomous systems need a principled unified approach to safety rather than only ad hoc fixes.
sections.title: Conclusion
